query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy, applying a two‐step heat treatment—initial solution treatment at ~1200 °C followed by controlled aging at ~800 °C for 2–10 hours—will induce the formation of a uniform distribution of nanoscale, coherent Ni3Ti precipitates that impede dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding, thereby significantly enhancing elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance relative to an alloy processed only with solution treatment.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy primarily composed of Ti and Ni (e.g., Ti 30 at%, Ni 30 at%, Cr 15 at%, Mo 15 at%, Al 10 at%) produced via casting and homogenization.
generation.intervention: A two‐step heat treatment: (1) a solution treatment at ~1200 °C for homogenization, and (2) a controlled aging treatment at ~800 °C for 2–10 hours to promote fine precipitate formation.
generation.conditions: Processing under an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; solution treatment at ~1200 °C followed by aging at ~800 °C for a controlled period (optimally between 2 and 10 hours) with continuous monitoring to avoid excessive precipitate coarsening.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, coherent Ni3Ti precipitates (or similarly structured intermetallic phases) uniformly dispersed within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: The fine precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion and inhibit grain‐boundary sliding, thus increasing the alloy's resistance to deformation (yield strength) and creep at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the alloy processed only with solution treatment, the two‐step heat-treated alloy will exhibit significantly higher yield strength and improved creep resistance at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: The same Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloy in an as-solutionized state without subsequent aging treatment.
generation.boundary: The alloy composition must remain within the high-entropy regime (each element 5–35 at%) and the processing temperatures must not exceed the specified limits to avoid undesirable phase transformations; aging times longer than 10 hours might produce coarser precipitates that could reduce strengthening.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of improvement is sensitive to the precise aging temperature and duration; optimization is required to balance precipitate formation and coarsening. There is some uncertainty regarding the exact precipitate size distribution and its stability under prolonged high-temperature exposure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloy. Subject one set to the two‐step heat treatment (solution treatment at ~1200 °C followed by aging at ~800 °C for 2–10 hours) and the other set to only solution treatment (control). Conduct high-temperature mechanical tests on both sets.
measurements: High-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength
Creep tests under constant load to evaluate creep resistance
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to assess precipitate size, distribution, and coherence
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to verify phase formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the aged alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance compared to the as-solutionized control, or if TEM/SEM reveals that the precipitate structure is unstable (e.g., coarsened) under the set aging conditions.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe effect of Al and Ti additions on the microstructure and properties of CoNiFe alloys was studied in this paper. The investigations were conducted on four specially designed and produced arc furnace alloys (from 3 to 5 components, with medium to high entropy). Samples in various states were analyzed, i.e., as-cast, after homogenization, after solution heat treatment, and after solution heat treatment and aging. The obtained samples were characterized by: SEM observations, EDS, XRD, TEM analyses, and finally, hardness measurements. The solid solution strengthening coming from the addition of 5 at. pct. Al was negligible, while the effect from the 5 at. pct. of Ti addition was significant. The precipitation hardening effect related to the presence of the (CoNi)3Ti phase caused by the Ti addition is comparable with the total effect of the Al and Ti addition, which caused the precipitation of (NiCo)3AlTi.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, heat treatment, aging, microstructure, mechanical properties

cited_evidence.text: The CALPHAD calculations indicate that oxygen can substantially affect the phase stability in Ti-V-Nb-Ta. In the absence of oxygen, equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta is predicted to exhibit a single-phase BCC structure, while trace levels of oxygen facilitate the formation of the α-Ti phase at the aging temperature, consistent with oxygen’s role as an α-stabilizer in Ti alloy (). As nitrogen is also an α-stabilizer in Ti alloys, it may play a similar role to oxygen in facilitating the formation of α-Ti phase in the Ti-V-Nb-Ta. Grain boundary α-Ti precipitates are observed to nucleate initially, followed by the formation of intragranular precipitates and the emergence of PFZs adjacent to the grain boundaries. The experimental characterization and equilibrium phase calculations lead to the inference that the formation of PFZ in the Ti-V-Nb-Ta system is the result of diffusion of Ti and major interstitials (O and N) to grain boundaries, with subsequent formation of nitrogen- and oxygen-rich α-Ti precipitates at the aging temperature. proposals.material_system: High-entropy alloy with primary constituents Ti and Ni (e.g., Ti 30 at%, Ni 30 at%, Cr 15 at%, Mo 15 at%, Al 10 at%)
proposals.intervention: A two‐step heat treatment that includes solution treatment followed by controlled aging
proposals.conditions: Solution treatment at ~1200 °C for homogenization, then aging at ~800 °C for 2–10 hours
proposals.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, coherent Ni3Ti (or similar) precipitates in the matrix
proposals.mechanism: The in situ formation of finely dispersed intermetallic precipitates impedes dislocation motion and grain‐boundary sliding at elevated temperatures, thereby providing precipitation strengthening
proposals.predicted_outcome: Enhanced yield strength and creep resistance at elevated temperatures relative to the same alloy in the as-solutionized state
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By deliberately activating a precipitation strengthening mechanism through aging, this intervention targets the high-temperature mechanical performance of Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloys, an area not previously explored when both are primary constituents.

proposals.material_system: High-entropy alloy with primary Ti and Ni (e.g., Ti 30 at%, Ni 30 at%, Cr 20 at%, Mo 10 at%, Al 10 at%)
proposals.intervention: Thermomechanical processing via severe plastic deformation
proposals.conditions: Apply cold rolling to achieve ~90% thickness reduction at room temperature followed by a short annealing treatment at ~600 °C for 30 minutes
proposals.structural_mediator: Ultrafine grain structure with increased high-angle grain boundaries and solute segregation at boundaries
proposals.mechanism: Grain-boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch effect) is enhanced by refining the grain size and stabilizing grain boundaries via segregation of alloying elements; this inhibits dislocation movement and grain-boundary sliding at high temperatures
proposals.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance relative to a conventionally processed (coarser grained) alloy
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This direction exploits microstructural refinement and grain boundary engineering to enhance high-temperature properties, providing an alternative approach for Ti- and Ni-based high-entropy alloys where traditional roles of Ti and Ni are expanded from mere additions to primary strengthening constituents.

proposals.material_system: Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloy substrate (e.g., Ti 28 at%, Ni 28 at%, Cr 20 at%, Mo 12 at%, Al 12 at%)
proposals.intervention: Application of a thin, protective ceramic coating
proposals.conditions: Deposit a ~5 μm thick Al2O3 (or YSZ) coating via physical vapor deposition at ~400 °C; follow with high-temperature exposure tests at ~900 °C
proposals.structural_mediator: A stable, diffusion-resistant surface layer acting as a barrier
proposals.mechanism: By limiting surface oxidation and degradation at high temperatures, the ceramic coating preserves the substrate’s microstructure and reduces the initiation of deformation or fatigue, indirectly enhancing elevated-temperature mechanical properties
proposals.predicted_outcome: Extended operational lifetime and improved creep performance compared to an uncoated alloy when exposed to similar high-temperature conditions
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention addresses the degradation mechanisms that can undermine high-temperature mechanics by protecting the alloy’s surface, which is crucial for advancing the performance of Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy systems under extreme environments.

proposals.material_system: High-entropy alloy with primary constituents Ti and Ni (e.g., Ti 25 at%, Ni 25 at%, Hf 10 at%, Cr 20 at%, Mo 20 at%)
proposals.intervention: Microalloying with a refractory element (Hf) to induce in situ nanoprecipitate formation
proposals.conditions: Cast to a homogeneous solid solution followed by aging at ~850 °C for 5 hours to promote Hf-rich nanoprecipitate formation
proposals.structural_mediator: Nanoscale Hf-rich precipitates dispersed uniformly in the matrix
proposals.mechanism: The Hf-rich particles act as obstacles to dislocation motion and help stabilize the microstructure at high temperatures through precipitate hardening, effectively enhancing the creep resistance and yield strength
proposals.predicted_outcome: Enhanced mechanical performance at elevated temperatures with higher yield strength and creep resistance compared to a baseline alloy without Hf microalloying
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: Using Hf as a microalloying element leverages its capacity to form stable, high melting nanoprecipitates. This novel composition approach directly targets the improved high-temperature behavior of alloys where Ti and Ni are primary, thus filling a gap in the existing studies

critiques.addresses_problem: The intervention directly targets the gap of improved high‐temperature mechanical properties in Ti‐ and Ni‐primary high-entropy alloys by introducing a microalloying element that forms in situ nanoprecipitates.
critiques.constraints: The proposed composition and heat treatment conditions are consistent with the allowed compositional range and processing constraints; however, Hf is already present in the given composition and is now being proposed as a microalloying addition, which requires clarity to avoid overlap with the baseline composition.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism of precipitate strengthening via the formation of nanoscale Hf-rich precipitates is physically sound, provided that Hf has a limited solubility in the matrix and precipitates at the specified aging condition.
critiques.feasibility: The casting, homogenization, and aging treatments at ~850 °C for 5 hours are standard procedures that can feasibly promote nanoprecipitate formation.
critiques.evidence: The provided records (PMC8074761 and PMC10532893) support the use of precipitate formation to enhance yield strength and creep resistance in related high-entropy alloys, though the evidence primarily discusses Co/Ni-induced sigma phases rather than Hf-rich precipitates.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk lies in the potential that Hf may not consistently form uniformly distributed, nanoscale precipitates without coarsening, which could diminish the strengthening effect.
critiques.fix: Clarify the Hf content as a trace microalloying addition distinct from its baseline presence, and optimize the aging parameters to ensure stable, uniformly distributed nanoprecipitates.

critiques.addresses_problem: The intervention aims to improve high-temperature properties by refining the grain structure and enhancing grain-boundary strengthening, which is a plausible approach for Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloys.
critiques.constraints: The proposed thermomechanical processing method respects the compositional system and operating conditions; however, care must be taken to ensure that the ultrafine grain structure remains stable at elevated temperatures.
critiques.physical_soundness: Utilizing severe plastic deformation to refine the grain structure is a well-known mechanism (Hall–Petch effect) for strength enhancement, but at high temperatures, ultrafine grains might be prone to grain growth or enhanced grain-boundary sliding.
critiques.feasibility: The cold rolling and short annealing treatment are established techniques in materials processing, making the intervention feasible with current methods.
critiques.evidence: The evidence from PMC10744552, PMC9506522, and PMC5494191 supports microstructural refinement for increased strength; however, the long-term stability of ultrafine grains under high-temperature exposure remains a concern.
critiques.main_risk: The ultrafine grain structure may not be thermally stable at elevated temperatures, leading to grain coarsening and loss of the intended strengthening benefits.
critiques.fix: Incorporate strategies to pin grain boundaries (e.g., minor additions that segregate to boundaries) or adjust the annealing step to stabilize the ultrafine structure against coarsening.

critiques.addresses_problem: The intervention seeks to improve elevated-temperature performance by mitigating surface degradation through the application of a ceramic coating, which indirectly preserves the alloy's mechanical properties.
critiques.constraints: While the coating does not alter the bulk composition and meets operational criteria by protecting the surface, it shifts the focus from intrinsic material strengthening to surface protection.
critiques.physical_soundness: The concept of using a diffusion-resistant, oxide-forming ceramic layer (Al2O3 or YSZ) is physically sound for combating oxidation; however, it does not directly enhance yield strength or creep resistance in the alloy's bulk.
critiques.feasibility: Ceramic coatings deposited by physical vapor deposition are well established, making this approach experimentally feasible.
critiques.evidence: The literature (e.g., PMC9498035 and PMC11267391) supports the use of protective coatings for high-temperature oxidation resistance, but this evidence pertains more to corrosion and oxidation rather than intrinsic mechanical property enhancement.
critiques.main_risk: The principal risk is delamination or spallation of the coating due to thermal expansion mismatch, which could lead to localized degradation and fail to improve the alloy's high-temperature mechanical performance as intended.
critiques.fix: Improve the coating’s adhesion and match its thermal expansion coefficient more closely to that of the substrate to ensure long-term integrity under thermal cycling.

critiques.addresses_problem: The two‐step heat treatment is designed to activate a precipitation strengthening mechanism by forming nanoscale, coherent Ni3Ti (or similar) precipitates, directly addressing the open challenge in Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloys.
critiques.constraints: The proposed thermal processing (solution treatment followed by controlled aging) fits within the composition and temperature ranges allowed and does not compromise the essential alloy properties.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism of precipitation strengthening via in situ formation of Ni3Ti precipitates is well supported by thermodynamic and kinetic principles in similar alloy systems, as evidenced by the literature.
critiques.feasibility: High-temperature solution treatment and controlled aging are standard industrial practices, making this intervention highly feasible with established methods.
critiques.evidence: Records from PMC10532893 and PMC10708198 support precipitation hardening in high-entropy systems with Ti and Ni additions, reinforcing the validity of this approach.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is the sensitivity of the precipitate size distribution; if the aging treatment is not optimally controlled, coarsening may occur, reducing the strengthening benefit.
critiques.fix: Conduct a detailed optimization study of aging temperature and time to finely tune the precipitate size and distribution for maximum strengthening without coarsening.

decision.rationale: Direction D directly addresses the challenge by promoting precipitation strengthening through a two-step heat treatment that is designed to form nanoscale, coherent Ni3Ti (or similar) precipitates in a Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloy. Although the critic noted that precise control of aging parameters is needed to avoid precipitate coarsening, this concern is fixable by a dedicated optimization study. The literature evidence from PMC10532893 and PMC10708198 supports the use of controlled aging to enhance high-temperature mechanical properties, making this approach the most promising.
